doc.title: Bob Rosengarden interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 6, 1996

title: Fewer jobs, jazz education, and Goodman's music in Japan
summary: He laments fewer jobs for young musicians, and marvels at Japanese audiences embracing American jazz.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You know a lot of the gentlemen that we’ve talked to that are in their eighties and so forth, like Buddy Tate, they all mentioned that when they were coming up, everyone was striving for an individual sound.
And I don’t know if that’s happening now. I don’t want to sound old-fashioned, but—

Well first of all there were many more musicians, there were more jobs so therefore there were more musicians. There aren’t that many musicians anymore. Not that many jobs. I feel badly for kids in school here. I’m sure every once in a while someone’s going to come up and really turn out to be a player of one kind or another. I don’t know where the hell he’s going to work. I mean it used to be you can go to a night club, which is a job, you know, to support a family. But not anymore, unless you go to Vegas or a place like gambling casinos where they have shows. All the L.A. guys, the film studios got rid of. You know they are, a lot of them moved to Vegas. Billy Watrous I think just moved back to L.A. Carl Fontana, Frank Rosolino before he died, all those guys, all the L.A. guys. We see each other occasionally at jazz festivals, there are still a few here and there in Arizona and places like that.
So the idea of jazz education in a sense is wonderful but in another sense it’s like I don’t know where they’re going to go with this education except to educate more people.

You said it in a much nicer way than I would have. Because I see it doing this, getting less and less and less and less and less. It’s a shame because it’s our music, America’s popular music. And it’s one of the few things that we are respected for all over the world, American jazz. You would have thought that we were the second coming in Japan with the Benny Goodman thing. “Sing Sing Sing” and all that stuff. And it was a good band, it © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-

was a good swinging band and a lot of good players. And I found it inspiring when the people got up and danced and there were some young people there who had no reason to know Benny Goodman, well I guess because it was Western and their parents told them this was the truth, and did reasonably good business, I mean people showed up.
In a social sense that’s so interesting because here is music that was popular in the late 30s and the 40s and then we had World War II with these two nations against each other—
They just hated us, they didn’t hate our music, or at least the governments anyway. Oh everything changes. It’s one of the advantages of having funny colored hair, you realize that.
